title: Eigen-1: Token-Level Retrieval Without the Pause
one_liner: Instead of pausing reasoning to fetch facts one step at a time, weave knowledge into each reasoning step at the token level and let candidates repair each other's errors.
lead: Science problems need both deep reasoning and precise facts. Traditional approaches ask the model to pause, retrieve a fact (costing extra tokens and attention switches), then resume—like constantly looking up a phone number during a conversation. Eigen-1 fixes this by retrieving knowledge silently, token by token, during reasoning, and by letting multiple solution attempts repair each other's gaps.

problem.h2: The tool tax: pausing reasoning to fetch
paras: Solving a hard biology problem—counting how many organisms with a specific trait would result from genetic crossing—is not pure logic; it also requires precision facts (what is a Punnett square? what does this gene variant do?). Today's multi-step reasoning systems handle this by using agents: one agent acts as Proposer (tries to reason), another as Querier (decides when to look up a fact), and Retriever fetches it. But every time the Querier says 'I need a fact,' the model stops, fetches (costs ~8-10 extra tokens per pause), and resumes. For a complex genetic problem, this creates 8-10 interruptions, doubling the number of agent steps and breaking the flow of reasoning.

The second problem is that when multiple agents try the problem in parallel, their answers are averaged together. But averaging a strong solution (the right haplotype count) with weak ones (wrong counts) dilutes the right answer. Traditional multi-agent systems treat all candidates equally, discarding what one agent got right that another got wrong.

callout.html: Embed knowledge retrieval inside each reasoning step (no pauses), and let each candidate solution be actively repaired by borrowing correct reasoning from other candidates.

steps.text: Five agents begin reasoning on the problem in parallel.
At each token, a Monitor agent (a specialized reasoner) listens for implicit gaps.
When a gap is detected, facts are retrieved and woven into the reasoning stream without pausing.
Each candidate solution becomes an anchor; peer agents then refine it, filling gaps and fixing errors.
Hard reasoning tasks vote (consensus); retrieval tasks keep diverse answers. Best answer emerges.

object.h2: What the paper changes: when and where knowledge enters reasoning
paras: Traditional RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieves when an agent explicitly asks. Eigen-1 changes this: instead of pausing to retrieve, the Monitor agent listens inside the reasoning stream itself, at the token level, and decides when facts are needed without interrupting. The knowledge injection happens embedded in the flow, not as a separate pause-and-fetch step.

hidden.h2: The tool tax: cost of explicit retrieval
hidden.name: Tool Tax (tokens and steps wasted by pausing)
paras: Every time an agent says 'I need a fact,' the system pauses reasoning, runs a retrieval step (costs tokens), and resumes. For a genetics problem needing 8-10 lookups, this tool tax is real: ~double the number of agent steps and 53.5% higher token usage than the baseline without retrieval.

The paper estimates this tool tax by comparing three configurations: no retrieval (fast but wrong), explicit retrieval (slower, more tokens, but accurate), and implicit retrieval (Eigen-1: accurate AND fast). The hidden quantity is the overhead—how many extra tokens and steps are wasted by the interruption itself, independent of the reasoning quality.

heat.caption: Darker means higher tool tax or better outcome. Boxes mark the explicit pause (costly) vs. implicit retrieval (efficient).

reads.html: The tool tax is the extra tokens and agent steps burned just by pausing to retrieve, before counting reasoning quality. Implicit retrieval eliminates these pauses.

The paper quantifies tool tax as the difference between token count and agent step count in explicit-retrieval configurations vs. implicit (Monitor-based) configurations. Eigen-1 shows 53.5% token reduction and 43.7% step reduction.

mechanism.h2: Why implicit retrieval at token level beats explicit pauses
paras: Explicit retrieval asks the model to reason, then stop and decide 'I need a fact,' then wait for retrieval, then resume. Each pause is a context switch: the model must remember what it was thinking, accept new tokens (the retrieved fact), and re-engage. This disruption compounds with each pause.

Eigen-1's Monitor operates inside the token stream. As the model generates each reasoning token, the Monitor listens and asks: 'Is there a knowledge gap here?' If yes, knowledge is retrieved and injected into the next tokens in the stream, without a pause. The reasoning continuity is preserved—facts flow in like water through a conversation, not like an interrupting phone call.

On top of this substrate, the Hierarchical Solution Refinement layer adds: instead of averaging five candidate solutions equally, Eigen-1 designates one as the 'anchor' and lets the other four repair it. This repair process is iterative—each candidate takes a turn as anchor, and peers fix its errors (logical gaps, arithmetic mistakes, wrong method choices). Hard reasoning tasks (logic, multi-step deduction) benefit from consensus (all five agents voting on the final step), while retrieval tasks benefit from diversity (keeping all five candidate answers for retrieving different knowledge paths). The Quality-Aware Iterative Reasoning layer adapts the refinement depth based on solution quality: if most anchors are already good, fewer repair cycles are needed.

stages.s: Five proposers start reasoning in parallel
Monitor detects knowledge gap (genetic method needed)
Knowledge injected into token stream (no pause)
Hierarchical repair: each candidate serves as anchor, peers fix errors
Quality-aware routing: consensus on reasoning, diversity on retrieval
Accurate answer, 53.5% fewer tokens, no lost coherence

math.h2: The repair penalty and quality weighting
math.words: quality_weighted_penalty = sum over all candidates (quality_score * distance_to_consensus + repair_depth_cost)
math.equation: L = sum_c quality_c * (||anchor_c - repaired_c|| + alpha * depth_c)
symbols: total loss (error penalty) across all repair iterations
a candidate solution (one of the five proposers)
how close candidate c is to the correct answer (measured from intermediate checks)
solution c when it serves as the anchor to be repaired
solution c after peers have fixed its gaps and errors
how much change happens during repair (distance moved)
weight controlling how much extra repair is beneficial vs. wasteful
how many repair cycles were applied to candidate c

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Candidate 1 (strong): quality_1 = 0.9, anchor error 0.3, repair reduces it to 0.05, depth = 2 cycles. Penalty = 0.9 * (0.3 - 0.05) + 0.5 * 2 = 0.9 * 0.25 + 1.0 = 0.225 + 1.0 = 1.225.
Candidate 2 (weak): quality_2 = 0.4, anchor error 0.7, repair reduces it to 0.2, depth = 3 cycles. Penalty = 0.4 * (0.7 - 0.2) + 0.5 * 3 = 0.4 * 0.5 + 1.5 = 0.2 + 1.5 = 1.7.

High-quality candidate 1 benefits from repair (error drops 0.25), but the cost is modest because quality_1 discounts wasted effort on weak repairs. Low-quality candidate 2 pays more repair cost relative to gain, so fewer cycles are devoted to it.

math.note: The formula ensures that strong candidates are refined deeply (because their quality is high), while weak candidates are refined sparingly (because effort spent on them yields low gain), and all repair uses Monitor-detected knowledge rather than explicit retrieval pauses.

bars.h2: Accuracy vs. efficiency: Eigen-1 breaks the tradeoff

charts.title: Baseline with explicit retrieval
charts.note: Explicit retrieval (pausing to fetch facts) achieves 34.9% accuracy but burns tokens and disrupts reasoning.

charts.title: Eigen-1 with implicit retrieval and hierarchical repair
charts.note: Implicit Monitor-based retrieval and iterative repair recover accuracy (+13.4 points) while halving tokens and maintaining coherence.

items.html: If the Monitor is too sensitive to knowledge gaps, it retrieves facts that are not needed, wasting tokens and diluting reasoning. The paper's solution: use a learned threshold tuned on a validation set.

If a candidate is already very accurate, additional repair cycles may introduce errors rather than fix them (the peer agents might be wrong). The paper mitigates this by making repair depth adaptive: high-quality candidates stop early.

items.b: Retrieval backend is weak or outdated.
items.html: The Monitor can only inject knowledge that exists in the retrieval index. If the index lacks a specific fact, the Monitor cannot help, because Monitor has no way to generate knowledge it has not seen—it can only recognize when reasoning needs knowledge and fetch it from memory. The paper tests on current datasets (HLE, SuperGPQA, TRQA) and uses HippoRAG as a strong baseline retrieval system to ensure the index is rich.

The paper shows that when Monitor sensitivity and repair depth are tuned, Eigen-1 achieves the highest reported accuracy (48.3%) on Humanity's Last Exam Bio/Chem Gold, with no loss in coherence and 53.5% fewer tokens than baseline RAG.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment with three configurations: (1) a baseline agent without any retrieval (gets logic right, facts wrong), (2) an explicit-retrieval agent (pauses to fetch, coherence suffers), and (3) Eigen-1 with Monitor-based retrieval and one hierarchical repair cycle. Use a mini-benchmark of 20 genetics or chemistry problems that require both reasoning (logical steps to solve a Punnett square) and retrieval (the correct definition of a allele, the right formula for hardy-weinberg equilibrium). Measure accuracy, token count, and a coherence score (do the reasoning steps flow naturally or do they show signs of pause-and-resume disruption?). The demo must make clear that Eigen-1 recovers the accuracy of explicit retrieval while keeping the token efficiency of no-retrieval reasoning.
demo.metric_eq: coherence_gain = accuracy_eigen1 - accuracy_baseline; efficiency_gain = tokens_explicit_retrieval - tokens_eigen1; shown_benefit = coherence_gain > 0 AND efficiency_gain > 0.4 * tokens_explicit_retrieval
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when a single run shows that Eigen-1 answers correctly, uses fewer tokens than pausing to retrieve, and reads like continuous reasoning.
